**The Whisper of the Forgotten Library**

There’s a library in the city that no one visits anymore. It stands on a quiet corner, its stone facade weathered by decades of rain and the indifferent brush of time. The doors are never locked, but they creak when opened, as if sighing at the rarity of a visitor. Inside, the air is thick with the scent of old paper, dust, and something else—something almost alive, like the faint hum of a half-remembered dream.

The books here are not arranged by author or title. They seem to shift when no one is looking, as if rearranging themselves for the next curious soul who might wander in. Some are bound in leather so cracked it flakes like autumn leaves under your fingers. Others have covers of cloth so faded you can no longer read the gold-embossed letters. A few have no spines at all, their pages held together by sheer stubbornness.

I came here by accident one afternoon, seeking shelter from a sudden downpour. The moment I stepped inside, the rain stopped, as if the sky itself had been waiting for me to find this place. The silence was so complete it felt like a presence, pressing gently against my ears.

Then I heard it—a whisper.

Not in any language I recognized, but in the way a breeze might speak if it carried memories instead of air. It came from a narrow aisle in the far corner, where the light from the stained-glass windows pooled in bands of blue and amber on the floor. There, on a shelf low to the ground, was a book with no title. Its cover was the color of twilight, and when I pulled it free, the whisper swelled, wrapping around me like a long-lost melody.

I opened it.

The pages were blank.

Not empty—*blank*, as if waiting. As if *knowing*. The whisper grew louder, and suddenly, I understood: this book was for stories that had never been told. For the words that got stuck in throats, the confessions that died on lips, the dreams that dissolved with the morning light. It was a vessel for all the things the world had forgotten to remember.

I don’t know how long I stood there. Time behaves strangely in that library. When I finally placed the book back on the shelf, the whisper faded, but it left something behind—a warmth in my chest, like the first sip of tea on a cold day. As I turned to leave, I noticed something I hadn’t seen before: a small, unmarked door at the end of the aisle. It hadn’t been there when I entered.

I didn’t open it.

Some secrets are meant to stay between the pages.

But I go back to the library sometimes, just to sit in the quiet. And if you ever find yourself there, listen closely. You might hear the whisper too. It might even have your name in it.
